editor_spans.body: I need to correct what I wrote last week. I said Westminster had no power to hand Scotland's regions anything and could only shame Holyrood into doing it. The full speech shows a real lever. Local government is devolved, but employment support and UK research and innovation money are not. Andy Burnham offered both: 'DWP devolution', and a say for Scotland's regions over where UK research and development money goes, as English mayors already have. This is something Westminster can actually give, and it hands Holyrood a choice it can't easily turn down. If it accepts, it has to pass the money and power on to the regions, not keep it in Edinburgh. That is the price Burnham is attaching.

The model Burnham wants to scale up is Scottish. He says he took what he saw at Easterhouse in 2023 back to Greater Manchester as 'Live Well', and is now offering to send it back north. But the speech itself explains why it worked. It was 'run by the local community and the people on the estate', with support built around each young person, including their clothes and travel. Now he wants it to be 'not a project on one estate, but the way we support everybody, everywhere.' That is the hard part. Every national employment programme has started out promising to treat people as individuals and ended up with targets and tick-boxes, the 'computer says no' approach he complains about. The deeper cause is that Treasury and DWP money comes with the need to account for it, and counting people pushes services back towards treating them as numbers. The test is whether any money passed down comes with the freedom not to measure success by job starts, not how much power is passed down.

The Ravenscraig and Leigh passages were not just scene-setting. They are his argument for why this is needed. Burnham says closures were 'taken hundreds of miles away' with no plan for what came next, and that thirty years later the Ravenscraig site is still being filled. If that explains the one-in-six young people not in work, education or training, the gap between Glasgow and East Renfrewshire in how long people live, and Dundee's empty shops, then the cure takes a generation. It won't fit a single parliament, and certainly not a meeting of the National Economic Council in a fortnight. His own warning that 'growth won't wait' runs against his own account of how long the damage takes to repair.

Story 509, the Editor's, made 2026-10-24: "The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning."; cited by no later Editor's Span
  S355 (the Editor's): The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning.
